nc_cereal_wall.blurb: A large south-facing slab on the Rumbling Bald massif above Hickory Nut Gorge, tucked just beyond the busier Cereal Buttress. The 20 climbs are almost all traditional, with a single bolted line and one aid route, and most of them are two or three pitches long, which makes this one of the better places on the Bald to string together longer outings. Grades run from 5.6 up to the 5.11 range, with the bulk sitting between 5.9 and 5.10. A path follows the base of the wall, so moving between routes is easy. Being exposed to the south, it is a pleasant spot for sunny days outside the hottest part of the year.

ns_1_deep_south_end.blurb: Deep South End is the first stretch of cliff you meet on reaching the lake below Mainface, the tallest and most extensive crag on the Nova Scotia mainland, east of Halifax. It holds 25 routes in monzogranite, a mix of trad (15) and sport (10). The grades cover a wide range, from 5.6 to 5.12, with most lines at 5.10 and above, so it suits stronger climbers best. Several routes carry runout or serious-fall warnings, and the wider cliff has an adventurous, sometimes dirty feel. Expect a real walk in through the woods before you reach the base.

ns_first_face.blurb: A single-pitch cliff in the Musquodoboit Harbour area east of Halifax, with 25 routes mostly around 25 metres long. The granite here is better than the local norm, with flat, positive holds and decent friction. Trad (15) outnumbers sport (9), with one aid line. Difficulty is concentrated in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, plus a few at 5.12 and only a handful of easier lines, so beginners often look to other nearby crags. The face catches plenty of sun when the weather is cool and dries quickly after rain. On still summer days the bugs can be heavy; a breeze helps a lot.

ns_the_skapper.blurb: A quiet woodland crag near St. Margarets Bay, west of Halifax, built around one steep, continuous, fairly flat face split by cracks and small dihedrals. Of the 22 routes, 19 are trad and three are sport, and the protection is mostly good. Grades start around 5.4 and reach 5.11, but the real concentration is in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, so it rewards a climber with some trad mileage. The setting is secluded and sheltered from wind, which keeps it calm but also buggy; mid-summer into early autumn is the more comfortable stretch. The walk in is through the forest and takes a good while.

ns_main_cliff.blurb: The largest section of Eagle's Nest, a small urban crag in the Bedford area close to Halifax. The rock is smooth and fractured, arranged in several short tiers. Its 22 routes are a fairly even mix of trad (12) and sport (10), mostly between 5.5 and 5.9, with a few harder lines up to the 5.11 range, which makes it a good fit for newer leaders and quick after-work sessions. A trail leads to the top of the cliff from a short drive along neighbourhood streets, and the usual way to the base is to circle around to the west end and walk back along the foot of the wall.

ns_a_e_gully.blurb: E-Gully sits at the north end of the North Buttress on Mainface, east of Halifax, and is partly cut off from the rest of the cliff by the lake, so it feels like a crag of its own. It has the steepest and hardest climbing on the wall: 20 routes split evenly between sport and trad, ranging from 5.6 up to 5.13, with most of the weight at 5.10 and above. Much of the sport climbing is a single pitch in the upper section, while a few trad lines and a longer multi-pitch route begin lower down. Reaching it takes a hike through the woods and then a scramble along the base beside the lake.
